Explanation: These agents can cause drug-induced pulmonary injury that may progress to fibrosis; frequency, mechanism, and predominant pattern differ by drug.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Medications causing lung fibrosis; Fibrogenic drug toxicity; Pneumotoxic drugs
Source Section: Restrictive Lung Disease > Pulmonary Fibrosis; PDF p. 58
Notes: All four are established pneumotoxic agents (FDA labels: bleomycin and amiodarone carry boxed warnings for pulmonary toxicity/fibrosis; busulfan label describes pulmonary fibrosis; methotrexate label warns of interstitial pneumonitis). QUALIFIER: methotrexate injury is predominantly acute/subacute hypersensitivity pneumonitis; chronic progressive fibrosis is less certain, so do not imply equal fibrotic risk. Board overlap: all except amiodarone are antineoplastic/immunosuppressive; amiodarone anchors the toxicity category. Added refs: FDA labels; Weiss & Muggia, Am J Med 1980.

Connection Title: Paraneoplastic syndromes of small cell lung carcinoma
Explanation: Small cell carcinoma may cause ectopic hormone secretion or antibody-mediated attack on neural targets, producing these four syndromes.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Small cell paraneoplastic effects; Small cell lung cancer syndromes
Source Section: Lung Cancer > Small Cell Carcinoma; PDF p. 63
Notes: All four are recognized SCLC paraneoplastic syndromes (NCCN SCLC 2026; Kim et al., JAMA 2025). SIADH is the most common endocrine syndrome; ectopic ACTH 2-6%; LEMS ~2-3% (anti-P/Q-type VGCC); paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration <1% (often anti-Hu, may coexist with LEMS). Associations are ''can occur,'' not universal. Ectopic ACTH correctly specifies the tumor-related form of Cushing syndrome.

Connection Title: Markers of neuroendocrine differentiation in small cell carcinoma
Explanation: These four can support neuroendocrine differentiation in small cell carcinoma; they are supportive rather than specific or uniformly positive.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Small cell neuroendocrine markers; Neuroendocrine tumor markers
Source Section: Lung Cancer > Small Cell Carcinoma; PDF p. 63
Notes: Chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and CD56 are the standard IHC neuroendocrine panel. QUALIFIER: NSE is chiefly a serum marker with poor IHC specificity and is NOT part of recommended IHC diagnostic panels (NCCN excludes NSE from NE IHC diagnosis; INSM1 is the emerging preferred marker). CD56 also labels NK cells. Board overlap: these markers also stain carcinoid and LCNEC. Added refs: NCCN SCLC 2026; Rudin et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021; Loy et al., Am J Surg Pathol 1995.

Explanation: These phases describe the classic progression from vascular congestion through cellular alveolar exudates to clearance.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Lobar pneumonia phases; Classic pneumococcal pneumonia stages
Source Section: Lung Pathology Fundamentals > Introduction to Respiratory Infections; PDF p. 41
Notes: Classic four-stage sequence verified (Torres et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021; Tuomanen et al., NEJM 1995). QUALIFIER: this is the classic pathological sequence, not a required time course in treated patients, and stages may coexist regionally within the same lobe (Zinserling et al., Infection 2022).

Explanation: Each is linked to an inhaled occupational inorganic dust or fiber; tissue responses vary.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pneumoconioses; Inorganic occupational lung diseases
Source Section: Restrictive Lung Disease > Pneumoconiosis; PDF p. 59
Notes: All four are inorganic occupational exposures. QUALIFIER: tissue responses differ (coal macules; silicotic nodules; asbestos interstitial fibrosis), and berylliosis (chronic beryllium disease) is a cell-mediated granulomatous hypersensitivity rather than a simple fibrotic pneumoconiosis, so do not claim identical fibrosis/granuloma patterns. Added refs: Solbes & Harper, J Investig Med 2018.

Explanation: Respiratory muscle dysfunction limits lung expansion without primary injury to the alveolar-capillary membrane.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Neuromuscular restrictive physiology; Respiratory muscle weakness disorders
Source Section: Restrictive Lung Disease > Restrictive Lung Disease Basics; PDF p. 57
Notes: All four cause extrapulmonary (neuromuscular) restriction: reduced TLC/VC with normal or elevated RV/TLC and preserved/normal FEV1/FVC. ''Neuromuscular causes of ventilatory failure'' is a synonymous framing, not a competing category. DLCO is typically preserved in extrapulmonary restriction but depends on measurement. Added refs: Stanojevic et al., ERS/ATS 2022; Wijdicks, Ann Neurol 2017.

Explanation: Fibrosis stiffens tissue; alveolar injury, surfactant dysfunction, and alveolar/interstitial fluid increase the difficulty of inflation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Stiff lung conditions; Reduced pulmonary compliance
Source Section: Respiratory Physiology Part One - Air > Compliance; PDF p. 18
Notes: All reduce compliance (Bos & Ware, Lancet 2022). QUALIFIER: early COVID-19 ARDS can show relatively preserved compliance despite severe hypoxemia; pulmonary edema reduces compliance by several mechanisms, not surfactant dilution alone. Board overlap: all also fit ''restrictive physiology'' and overlap with ARDS/NRDS pathology (PULM-021).

Connection Title: Factors shifting the oxygen dissociation curve right
Explanation: Each reduces hemoglobin oxygen affinity and promotes oxygen unloading at a given oxygen tension.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Reduced hemoglobin oxygen affinity; Rightward oxyhemoglobin shift
Source Section: Respiratory Physiology Part Two - Blood > Hemoglobin; PDF p. 28
Notes: Bohr-effect right shift (lower affinity, higher P50) confirmed (Hsia, NEJM 1998). Directional tiles are required; bare ''pH'' or ''temperature'' would not identify the effect. BOARD OVERLAP: this is the mirror image of PULM-009 (left shift) and the two should not appear on the same 16-tile board.

Connection Title: Factors shifting the oxygen dissociation curve left
Explanation: These directional changes increase hemoglobin oxygen affinity and reduce unloading at a given oxygen tension.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Increased hemoglobin oxygen affinity; Leftward oxyhemoglobin shift
Source Section: Respiratory Physiology Part Two - Blood > Hemoglobin; PDF p. 28
Notes: Left shift (higher affinity, reduced unloading) confirmed (Hsia, NEJM 1998). Carbon monoxide and fetal hemoglobin also left-shift the curve (not listed). BOARD OVERLAP: mirror image of PULM-008; do not place both on one board.

Connection Title: Hypoxemia mechanisms responsive to supplemental oxygen
Explanation: Supplemental oxygen can improve hypoxemia from each of these mechanisms, unlike a substantial pure right-to-left shunt.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Oxygen-responsive hypoxemia; Non-shunt mechanisms of hypoxemia
Source Section: Respiratory Physiology Part Two - Blood > A-a Gradient; PDF p. 36
Notes: These four respond to supplemental O2 whereas true right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0) does not (Wemple, Swenson & Swenson, NEJM Evid 2023). QUALIFIER: these are mechanisms, not guarantees of full correction; mixed shunt physiology blunts the response. ''Non-shunt hypoxemia'' is a synonymous framing, not a competing category.

Connection Title: Reduced oxygen delivery or use despite normal arterial oxygen tension
Explanation: A normal PaO2 can coexist with poor tissue oxygen delivery or utilization because dissolved oxygen does not reflect functional hemoglobin carriage or cellular oxygen use.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tissue hypoxia with normal PaO2; Normal oxygen tension does not exclude hypoxia
Source Section: Respiratory Physiology Part Two - Blood > Abnormal Oxygen Levels; PDF p. 33
Notes: All four can present with a normal PaO2. QUALIFIER: anemia, CO, and methemoglobinemia impair oxygen carriage; cyanide (and partly CO) impairs mitochondrial oxygen utilization (histotoxic) and need not reduce arterial oxygen content. Board overlap: broader ''causes of tissue hypoxia.'' Added refs: Henretig et al., NEJM 2019; Twine & Rees, Br J Haematol 2026.

Explanation: Sepsis and pancreatitis injure lung through systemic inflammation; pneumonia and acid aspiration act directly on lung tissue.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: ARDS precipitants; Diffuse alveolar damage triggers
Source Section: Lung Pathology Special Topics > ARDS and NRDS; PDF p. 74
Notes: Classic precipitants confirmed (Meyer et al., Lancet 2021; Matthay et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019). These are selected classic triggers, not exhaustive (trauma, transfusion/TRALI, shock, overdose also qualify). ''Aspiration'' here means chemical acid injury; distinguish from aspiration pneumonia.

Connection Title: Core obstructive lung diseases in the source
Explanation: These diseases can produce airflow limitation with a reduced FEV1/FVC through loss of recoil, mucus obstruction, or bronchoconstriction.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Obstructive pulmonary disorders; Diseases with obstructive spirometry
Source Section: Obstructive Lung Disease > Obstructive Lung Disease Basics; PDF p. 43
Notes: All produce obstructive spirometry. QUALIFIERS: asthma is characteristically reversible while emphysema/chronic bronchitis are largely irreversible; CF is obstructive but GOLD 2026 excludes it from the COPD definition; spirometry may normalize between asthma attacks (not always obstructed). Board overlap: ''air trapping disorders.'' Added refs: Stanojevic et al., ERS/ATS 2022; GOLD 2026; Postma & Rabe, NEJM 2015.

Tile 4: Congenital absence of the vas deferens
Explanation: CFTR dysfunction produces obstructed meconium, impaired pancreatic secretion, high sweat chloride, and a characteristic cause of male infertility.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cystic fibrosis clues; Multisystem CFTR manifestations
Source Section: Obstructive Lung Disease > Cystic Fibrosis; PDF p. 54, 55
Notes: All four are classic multisystem CF clues (sweat chloride >60 mmol/L is the diagnostic gold standard; CBAVD causes obstructive azoospermia). QUALIFIER: characteristic but not universal (milder genotypes may be pancreatic-sufficient; meconium ileus in ~12%). Added refs: Farrell et al. (CF Foundation), J Pediatr 2017; Mall et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2024.

Explanation: Loss of antiprotease protection drives early panacinar emphysema and a low serum AAT level, while retained polymerized Z-protein injures hepatocytes, producing PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules and cirrhosis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Alpha-1 antitrypsin disease; Pulmonary and hepatic AAT deficiency findings
Source Section: Obstructive Lung Disease > COPD > Emphysema; PDF p. 53
Notes: CORRECTION: original tiles ''panacinar emphysema'' and ''lower-lobe emphysema'' describe the same classic phenotype along two axes (lobular morphology vs anatomic distribution; basal predominance in only ~64% of Pi*ZZ), so they are near-redundant. Replaced ''lower-lobe emphysema'' with ''Decreased serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level'' (serum <11 microM; standard initial diagnostic test) as a distinct, independently supported clue. QUALIFIERS: classically emphysema in a young/nonsmoking patient; PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules are the hepatic histologic hallmark; necrotizing panniculitis is an alternative distinct clue. Replacement refs: Strnad et al., NEJM 2020; ATS/ERS Statement, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2003 (PMID 14522813). Original source supports only the emphysema/globule/cirrhosis claims, not the serum-level tile.

Connection Title: Findings supporting pulmonary squamous cell carcinoma
Explanation: Squamous differentiation produces keratin and desmosomal intercellular bridges; a central tumor and PTHrP-mediated humoral hypercalcemia are classic supporting clues.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Squamous lung carcinoma clues; Keratinizing lung carcinoma associations
Source Section: Lung Cancer > Non-Small Cell Carcinoma; PDF p. 64
Notes: Keratinization (keratin pearls) and intercellular bridges are WHO essential histologic criteria for squamous cell carcinoma; central location and PTHrP hypercalcemia are classic associations, not required findings. QUALIFIER: intercellular bridges may be absent in poorly differentiated tumors; peripheral SCC is increasingly common; hypercalcemia occurs in advanced disease. Added refs: Berezowska et al., Histopathology 2024; Guise & Wysolmerski, NEJM 2022.

Explanation: Asbestos can cause benign pleural disease (calcified plaques, benign effusion), malignant pleural mesothelioma, and parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Asbestos-related thoracic disease; Thoracic consequences of asbestos exposure
Source Section: Restrictive Lung Disease > Pneumoconiosis; PDF p. 59
Notes: REVISED to resolve the original ambiguity-2 HOLD: title changed from ''Thoracic findings'' to ''Intrathoracic manifestations of asbestos exposure'' to explicitly span pleural and parenchymal disease; generic ''Pleural effusion'' specified as ''Benign asbestos pleural effusion'' (effusions have many causes). All four are established asbestos consequences; competing category ''pleural disease'' captures only 3 of 4 (asbestosis is parenchymal), so it is not an equally strong category for the full set. BOARD-LEVEL OVERLAP WARNING: three tiles (plaques, benign effusion, mesothelioma) are pleural and could be grouped as ''asbestos pleural disease'' on a 16-tile board; pair with care and avoid a competing pleural category. Added refs: Solbes & Harper, J Investig Med 2018; Roach et al., Radiographics 2002; Gevenois et al., Eur Respir J 1998.

Tile 3: Bronchial breath sounds over peripheral lung
Explanation: Consolidated lung transmits voice and bronchial sounds differently and can cause dullness and crackles.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pneumonia examination findings; Physical signs of consolidation
Source Section: Lung Pathology Fundamentals > Lung Physical Exam; PDF p. 38
Notes: Classic consolidation signs confirmed (Wipf et al., Arch Intern Med 1999; Bohadana et al., NEJM 2014). QUALIFIER: crackles and dullness are nonspecific; if airways are obstructed by secretions, breath sounds are decreased rather than bronchial; a coexisting pleural effusion alters expected fremitus. Board overlap: ''pneumonia'' as a clinical syndrome and shared dullness/fremitus with effusion (PULM-019).

Tile 4: Contralateral tracheal shift with a large effusion
Explanation: Pleural fluid dampens percussion and sound transmission; a sufficiently large collection may displace the mediastinum away from the effusion.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pleural fluid examination findings; Large pleural effusion signs
Source Section: Lung Pathology Special Topics > Pleural Effusion; PDF p. 72
Notes: Verified: dullness (summary +LR ~8.7), reduced breath sounds, reduced tactile fremitus (best rule-out, -LR ~0.21), and contralateral shift with a large effusion (Wong et al., JAMA 2009; Light, NEJM 2002). PRESERVE the large-effusion qualifier: shift is not obligatory and small effusions cause none. Distinguishing overlap: atelectasis shifts the trachea ipsilaterally (opposite direction).

Explanation: Pressurized pleural air impairs ipsilateral ventilation and venous return, producing an obstructive-shock pattern with possible mediastinal displacement.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tension pneumothorax examination; Pleural pressure causing obstructive shock
Source Section: Lung Pathology Special Topics > Pneumothorax; PDF p. 69
Notes: Verified (Roberts et al., Ann Surg 2015, systematic review). QUALIFIERS: tracheal deviation is relatively uncommon (~15-30%) and may be late or absent; hypotension is a late sign in spontaneously breathing patients but early in ventilated patients; tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis not requiring all signs. ''Obstructive shock'' fits the hemodynamic tile but is not an equally strong category for all four.

Connection Title: Features of diffuse alveolar damage in ARDS
Explanation: Alveolar-capillary injury permits protein leakage and hyaline membrane formation, while surfactant dysfunction contributes to stiff, collapse-prone lungs.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: ARDS alveolar pathology; Diffuse alveolar injury findings
Source Section: Lung Pathology Special Topics > ARDS and NRDS; PDF p. 74
Notes: Verified features of diffuse alveolar damage (Matthay et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019; Bos & Ware, Lancet 2022). QUALIFIER: hyaline membranes are a histologic (biopsy/autopsy) feature, not a bedside criterion, and DAD is found in only ~45-56% of Berlin-defined ARDS. BOARD OVERLAP: neonatal RDS shares hyaline membranes, surfactant dysfunction, and reduced compliance; overlaps with PULM-007 (reduced compliance). Separate carefully.
